title: Giving Constructive Feedback People Can Use
summary: Constructive feedback is feedback someone can act on. Say what you saw instead of a label, name the impact, make one clear ask, say why you care and follow up later.
author: Nguyen Le Phong
html:
You've spent ten minutes on one review comment, and your coffee has gone from warm to forgotten. The technical point is simple: the PR mixes a data migration with a UI change, and splitting them would make the rollout safer. The first draft says "This PR is a bit messy." You delete it. The second draft says what's in the PR, why splitting helps and what you'd suggest. That's the one you post.

Those ten minutes are most of what "constructive" means. The point stays exactly the same. You're just shaping it so the other person can do something with it.

Usable, and still honest

Kim Scott's Radical Candor gives a handy map. Good feedback means you "Care Personally and Challenge Directly at the same time." Drop the challenge and you get what she calls Ruinous Empathy, where you care but keep the criticism to yourself or sugar-coat it. Drop the care and you get Obnoxious Aggression: "You challenge, but you don't show you care."

Constructive feedback lives where both are present. If the person walks away feeling judged, your point may have been right, yet it probably won't change anything. If they walk away feeling fine with no idea what to change, the kindness only went halfway. You're aiming for someone who knows exactly what to try next and still wants to work with you.

This post is about giving that kind of feedback day to day. For the receiving side, see how to give feedback, and how to take it. For the conversations that feel genuinely hard, there's a script for difficult feedback.

Say what you saw, not the label

"Messy", "vague" and "not accountable" are labels. They tell the person how you feel about their work and leave them guessing about what happened. Describing the event lowers the temperature, because now both of you are looking at the same thing instead of arguing about character.

Then add why it matters. A big mixed PR slows review and makes rollback riskier. A vague ticket leaves QA guessing at acceptance criteria. A sharp message in a shared thread can teach a junior to stop asking questions early. Naming the impact also keeps you honest: if you can't name one, the point may just be your taste.

Last comes the ask, and it has to be something a person can actually do tomorrow. "Be more careful" isn't an ask. Here's how the three parts look together:

The label What you saw The ask
"This PR is messy." "This PR changes the schema, the API response and the dashboard copy in one release." "Can we ship the migration first, then the UI change in a second PR?"
"Your tickets are vague." "The last two tickets didn't say what output we expect, and QA asked about both." "Could you add one example input and the expected output to each ticket?"
"We're not accountable." "Yesterday's incident review ended without an owner for the database alert." "Before we leave the next review, let's put one name next to each action item."
"You're too harsh in Slack." "In the release thread, 'did anyone even test this?' came right after Linh's question." "When something looks untested, could you ask what was covered instead?"

Say why you're bothering

Critical feedback often raises a question in the receiver's head: does this person think I'm not good enough? A short sentence about why you're giving the feedback can answer it before it grows.

A 2014 study by David Yeager, Geoffrey Cohen and colleagues tested this with seventh graders. Teachers wrote critical comments on student essays, and each essay came with one of two notes. The control note said, "I'm giving you these comments so that you'll have feedback on your paper." The other said, "I'm giving you these comments because I have very high expectations and I know that you can reach them." Students could then choose whether to revise. Among African American students, an estimated 71% of those who got the second note revised their essays, versus 17% with the control note. White students showed a smaller trend in the same direction that wasn't statistically significant (Yeager et al., 2014).

That was 44 students in a school, not engineers in a sprint, so don't read it as a workplace rule. The authors argue the note worked by building trust: it told students the criticism came from high standards and belief in them, not from bias. In a team, the honest version sounds like "I'm flagging this because this module is going to be yours, and I think you can own it." Only say it if it's true. People can smell a formula.

Mind your weight and your timing

The same sentence lands differently depending on who says it. A peer saying "this is confusing" is a data point. A tech lead or the person who writes your promotion packet saying it can feel like a verdict. If you're senior, "just being direct" carries more force than you intend. That doesn't mean holding back. It means being precise, asking for context before assuming you know the whole story, and saying clearly which points are blocking and which are just ideas.

Timing matters as well. Feedback given in the heat of frustration carries extra weight that doesn't belong to the issue. Feedback saved up for months becomes a surprise at review time, and by then nobody remembers the details. Aim for close to the work and after you've cooled down: a review comment on the exact line, a short message after a tense meeting, five minutes in your next 1:1. Keep anything about behavior, as opposed to code, in private.

Follow up, and notice the change

Feedback without follow-up only moves pressure from your desk to theirs. If you asked someone to split their PRs, offer to pair on the first split. If you asked for clearer tickets, look at the next one together.

Then notice when it works. "The last release came in three small PRs, and review took a day instead of a week. Nice." That one sentence tells the person the change was seen and worth it. Kim Scott pairs criticism that's "kind and clear" with praise that's "specific and sincere," and the follow-up is where the praise naturally fits.

If the feedback is about code review specifically, How to Review Code Kindly goes deeper on wording and labels.

Try this week

  • Take one piece of feedback you've been putting off and write it as three lines: what you saw, why it matters, the ask.
  • Before you send it, check for labels like "messy", "careless" or "vague", and swap each for the event behind it.
  • If it's true, add one sentence about why you're bothering.
  • Put a reminder two weeks out to check back, and say something when you see the change.

faqs.a: The person can use it. Constructive feedback describes what happened, explains why it matters and ends with a concrete ask the person can act on soon. Kim Scott's Radical Candor frames it as caring personally and challenging directly at the same time.

faqs.q: How do I give critical feedback without sounding harsh?
faqs.a: Replace labels like 'messy' or 'vague' with the specific event you saw, explain the impact on the team or system, and make one request the person can act on tomorrow. If it's true, say why you're giving the feedback, for example that you think they can own the area.

faqs.q: Does explaining why I'm giving feedback really help?
faqs.a: There is evidence from schools. In a 2014 study of 44 seventh graders, essay comments came with a note saying the teacher had high expectations and believed the student could meet them. An estimated 71% of African American students who got that note revised their essays, versus 17% with a neutral note. It was a classroom study, so treat it as a useful hint rather than a workplace rule.

faqs.q: When should I give constructive feedback?
faqs.a: Close to the work and after you have cooled down. A review comment on the exact line, a short message after a meeting or a few minutes in your next 1:1 all work. Avoid saving feedback for months, and keep anything about behavior private.

faqs.q: What should happen after I give feedback?
faqs.a: Follow up. Offer help with the first attempt, check back after a week or two, and say something specific when you see the change. Without follow-up, feedback mostly just moves pressure onto the other person.
